questions.q: What computation does nn.Linear(in_features, out_features) perform?
options: y = max(0, x), applied elementwise
y = x @ weight.T + bias, a learned linear transformation of the last dimension of the input
y = x / out_features, a normalization
It applies a convolution over the input
questions.explain: nn.Linear learns a weight matrix and bias vector and computes y = x @ weight.T + bias, transforming the last dimension of the input from in_features to out_features.

questions.q: Why does stacking two nn.Linear layers with no activation function between them fail to add expressive power?
options: PyTorch raises an error if you try
Composing two linear functions produces another linear function, so the stack is mathematically equivalent to a single linear layer
Linear layers can only be used once per model
It actually does add expressive power, just more slowly
questions.explain: A linear function composed with another linear function is still linear overall. Without a non-linear activation in between, stacking linear layers provides no additional modeling capacity over a single layer.

questions.q: Why is ReLU typically preferred over Sigmoid or Tanh for hidden layers in deep networks?
options: ReLU always produces negative outputs
ReLU is cheap to compute and, unlike Sigmoid/Tanh, does not saturate for large positive inputs, which helps avoid vanishing gradients in deep networks
ReLU guarantees the loss will reach zero
ReLU is only usable on GPUs
questions.explain: Sigmoid and Tanh saturate (flatten out) for large-magnitude inputs, causing their gradients to shrink toward zero and slow learning in deep stacks. ReLU's gradient stays constant for positive inputs, which is cheaper and avoids much of that saturation problem.

questions.q: In a model ending with nn.Sigmoid() for a binary classification task, what does the output represent?
options: A raw, unbounded score with no interpretation
A value squashed into (0, 1), interpretable as a probability
A value squashed into (-1, 1), zero-centered
The gradient of the loss function
questions.explain: Sigmoid squashes any real input into the range (0, 1), which is why it's the natural final-layer choice for binary classification, where the output is interpreted as a probability.

questions.q: What does nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 1)) do when called with an input of shape (4, 10)?
options: It raises a shape error because Sequential cannot chain more than one layer
It runs the input through each layer in order -- Linear(10,32), then ReLU, then Linear(32,1) -- producing an output of shape (4, 1)
It runs all three layers in parallel and averages the results
It ignores the ReLU layer since it has no parameters
questions.explain: nn.Sequential feeds its input through each child module in the order they were added. Here the (4,10) input becomes (4,32) after the first Linear, passes through ReLU unchanged in shape, then becomes (4,1) after the final Linear.
